title: Chiasm
summary: A literary pattern in which corresponding elements are arranged symmetrically, often drawing attention to a center or contrast.
historical_context: Ancient oral and written compositions often used repetition, parallelism, and symmetry to organize material for memory, emphasis, and interpretation.
ancient_near_east_context: Chiasm appears in ancient Hebrew narrative and poetry as a literary ordering device, especially in parallel and concentric structures used for emphasis and memory.
hebraic_worldview: Biblical chiasm works within a Scripture-shaped habit of repetition, meditation, and patterned attention rather than a modern preference for linear outline only.
second_temple_context: Second Temple Jewish interpretation was attentive to repeated wording, narrative pattern, and scriptural echoes, providing a receptive environment for structured readings.
canonical_context: Chiasm can help readers observe literary design in narrative, poetry, and discourse, but it serves interpretation only when grounded in clear textual markers.
literary_context: Chiasm is a literary observation tool, not a doctrine; it should clarify flow, emphasis, and correspondence in a specific passage.
covenantal_significance: Chiastic structures may highlight covenant themes, but the structure itself does not create covenant meaning apart from the passage.
original_audience: Readers learning to observe biblical literary structure
canonical_role: Literary-device entry for recognizing and testing inverted parallel structure in biblical texts.
canonical_placement: A possible structure across multiple biblical genres
interpretive_disputes: Proposed chiasms vary in strength; some are clear from repeated language while others are speculative.

interpretive_notes.note: A strong chiasm should be supported by repeated words, matching ideas, clear boundaries, and interpretive payoff.
Do not force a chiasm onto every repeated pattern; ordinary parallelism and thematic repetition may explain the passage better.
